title: You are the Master
hook: too thaakur tum peh ardaas: You are the Master, to You this prayer; You are mother and father, we Your children

segments.voice: Yesterday, daataa, the giver: life, food and a body, all given, and the giver forgotten. Your line was remember the giver. Today, ashtpadi four reaches its last stanza.

A small child wakes in the night and calls out one word. Not a speech, not an explanation: just the name of the person who will come. The child doesn't wonder whether it's allowed, or whether the words are right, or whether the request is too small. It knows who to call. Ashtpadi four has spent its stanzas on the forgetful one: you were fed, clothed, carried, and you forgot. Then, in the eighth and last stanza, the voice changes. The scolding stops, and a child calls out.
screen: `A CHILD CALLS IN THE NIGHT.` → `ONE WORD, NO SPEECH.` → `THE SCOLDING STOPS.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens: too thaakur, tum peh ardaas. You are the Master; to You, this prayer. Thaakur is an old word for a lord or master, the one a household depends on. Ardaas is the word Sikhs still use for their standing prayer, said at the close of a gathering. So the first line names who God is, and says what's happening: asking. The next line, in plain words: soul and body are all Your capital, Your trust, held for a while. Then the line that gives today its carry: tum maat pitaa, ham baarik tere. You are mother and father; we are Your children. Notice the order: mother comes first. Guru Arjan reaches for an everyday bond, parent and child, and uses it for the One beyond all forms. A Master can feel far away. A mother is the one who comes when you call in the night. Next: in Your kindness are countless comforts. And the stanza holds both: the One higher than the highest, whose limit nobody knows, and the One as near as a parent's hand. The forgetful guest of the last few days isn't thrown out. The stanza ends with the guest finally speaking like a child at home. Guru Arjan closes ashtpadi four signing it Nanak, as the Gurus sign their hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib: Your servant, forever a sacrifice to You.
screen: `THAAKUR: THE MASTER OF THE HOUSE.` · `ARDAAS: TO YOU, THIS PRAYER.` · `SOUL AND BODY, ALL YOUR TRUST.` · `MOTHER AND FATHER; WE, YOUR CHILDREN.` · then, large: `MOTHER AND FATHER.`

segments.voice: Say the line once, slowly: tum maat pitaa, ham baarik tere, You are mother and father; we are Your children, as a prayer if you pray, or as a line of old poetry if you don't. Then breathe in with mother and father, breathe out with we, the children, and let your shoulders drop, the way they do when someone you trust walks into the room.
Thaakur, master or lord: too thaakur, the opening of ashtpadi four's last stanza, where the forgetful guest finally calls out like a child.
Your line: mother and father. A good last line to hear yourself say before sleep. Rest well.

howItsDone: This stanza closes the fourth ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib; it is often said standing, just before the Ardas, and some say it quietly at night.

original.note: Gurmukhi: thaakur, master or lord, the one a household depends on; the stanza's first word for God.

trapdoor: what you thought: calling God the Master sounds cold and far away.
what it means: the same stanza calls the Master mother and father, and us the children.
what a scholar hears: thaakur is an old Indic word for a lord; in the Guru Granth Sahib it is a name for God, and here it sits beside the language of family.

chat.says: Why does that Sukhmani prayer call God mother and father?
options: Because the One beyond all forms is also near, like a parent who comes when a child calls.
Because it's a polite title only; the stanza says God stays far away and is never near.
Because it's meant for children only; grown-ups use other words when they pray.
